properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Wish 19 from the dev_storyflow agent, 2026-09-05. Nothing is intent.

THE ASK, verbatim in intent: constructors should report ALL validation failures in one reply, and enum-typed fields should show their legal values on the FIRST rejection - not only when that specific field is the one that failed. Their case was four round-trips to record one ChangeEvent, each rejection revealing exactly one more rule the tool had known from the start.

WHY THIS IS HARDER THAN IT SOUNDS, and the reason it is an idea rather than a fix: the refusals are serde's own. The request structs carry deny_unknown_fields and serde deserialization stops at the FIRST error by design. Collecting every violation means either a second validation pass after a permissive parse, or hand-written deserializers, or a schema-level validator that runs before serde. Each of those is a real architectural choice for a surface of 150-plus tools.

DIRECTIONS, none chosen:

1. ENRICH THE UNKNOWN-FIELD REFUSAL FOR THE KNOWN COMMONEST MISTAKES. Intercept serde's unknown-field error, and when the field is one a tool description already calls the commonest mistake, append the one sentence that fixes it - for add_change_event, 'prose goes in summary; there is no description'. Cheapest by far; no change to parsing; and it moves the existing warning from the leg nobody reads to the leg everybody reads. Counter: it is per-tool hand maintenance of a list, which is the class of thing this project says rots.

2. SHOW THE ENUMS ON ANY REFUSAL. Whatever field failed, the reply also lists every enum-typed field on that request and its legal values. Cheap, generic, needs no per-tool list - the schema already knows which fields are enums. Counter: it lengthens every refusal, and the verbose-reply complaint from the same batch of reports cuts the other way.

3. A PERMISSIVE PARSE THEN A FULL VALIDATION PASS, returning every violation as a list. The real answer to the ask. Counter: it is the expensive one, it changes how every request struct is read, and it makes a refused call do MORE work than an accepted one.

4. NOTHING - the errors that enumerate values are already good, and the reporter said so. Counter: the third project in seventeen days made the same first mistake, and the documented fix was in place for all three.

THE MEASURED PART, which is why direction 1 leads: the mistake this would fix most was already fixed once, in the tool description, on 2026-08-19, and a third independent project made it on 2026-09-05. That is a controlled experiment on whether a description reaches a user mid-work, and the answer was no. The refusal is read at the moment it is needed; the description is not.

NOT ESTABLISHED: how much of the four-round-trip cost was the two GOOD errors. Two of the four already enumerated their values and were praised; if those are typical then direction 2 buys little, and the whole gain is in direction 1's single sentence. Nobody has counted how many constructors have a commonest-mistake warning that a serde refusal cannot repeat.
properties.name: OPEN — a constructor knows every rule on the first call and discloses them one per failure. Should a refusal report all violations at once, and show an enum's values before that field fails?
properties.rationale: Captured under the brainstorm skill; recorded as an idea, nothing promoted. Kept separate from the constructor-naming defect because that records what is inconsistent and this asks what a refusal should do about it. The measured half - a documented fix that a third project walked past - is recorded as its own fact so it survives whatever is decided here.
